quote: the concept of “currying,” named after the mathematician Haskell Curry
content: The name is Curry's; the idea isn't. Moses Schönfinkel published the technique of turning many-argument functions into one-argument functions that return functions in 1924. Frege anticipated it, and Curry himself credited Schönfinkel, which is why some call it "Schönfinkelization." A small point, but the essay rests its metaethical payoff on a formal device whose origin it gets wrong.

quote: An alternative and equally valid standpoint is that “sexiness” does refer to a one-place function—but each speaker uses a different one-place function
content: This is speaker relativism with the speaker's function fixed in place, and it inherits the objection that has dogged speaker relativism for decades: it loses disagreement (Dreier 1990). If Fred's "sexy" means Sexiness_20934 and Bloogah's means Sexiness_72546, they aren't disagreeing; each is right about a different function. That is harmless for sexiness and fatal for morality, where people who say "wrong" take themselves to be contradicting each other. Book V's metaethics ("Morality as Fixed Computation") is built on this device, and it never explains what moral disagreement between people with different fixed functions consists in.

quote: The whole confusingness of the subsequent philosophical debate rested on a tendency to instinctively curry concepts or instinctively uncurry them.
content: The distinction presented here as the key to dissolving the debate was worked out within that debate, decades earlier. Kaplan separated character, a function from contexts to contents, from content, which is currying applied to meaning (Kaplan, "Demonstratives," 1977/1989; book chapter, no DOI). Two-dimensional semantics developed the "world-eating" reading of "water" in detail (Chalmers, "The Foundations of Two-Dimensional Semantics," 2006; book chapter, no DOI). Putnam's own paper already separated what fixes reference from what is referred to (Putnam 1973). The debate didn't rest on confusion over currying. It was about which of the two functions is the meaning, and that question survives being told that both exist.

quote: try putting the above distinctions to work to Taboo such confusing words as “objective,” “subjective,” and “arbitrary.”
content: The currying device makes "objective" too cheap to be interesting. Any preference whatever, once curried, is a fixed function whose outputs "all observers can agree on," so a torturer's preferences are as objective in this sense as a saint's. If this is the objectivity morality has, and "Morality as Fixed Computation" says it is, then it is the objectivity every relativist already grants. The Taboo exercise relabels the dispute without resolving it.
